findings.description: The default argument `metadata: dict[str, str] = {}` is one dict shared by every call that omits `metadata`. Line 80 calls `setdefault` on it, so the first put without metadata stores its guessed content type in the shared default. Later calls that omit metadata keep that stale value because `setdefault` does not overwrite it. For example, put('a.pdf', ...) followed by put('b.png', ...) stores b.png with content-type application/pdf. The same `setdefault` also writes into a caller-supplied dict, so callers see their argument changed. Both are wrong results on a common path.
findings.suggestion: Use `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None`, then build a fresh dict: `meta = dict(metadata or {})` and `meta.setdefault("content-type", guess_content_type(key))`. Serialise `meta` instead of the argument.
findings.title: Mutable default dict leaks content-type between unrelated puts and mutates caller's dict

findings.description: The metadata file is atomically replaced at line 83 before the blob is written at lines 84-86. If `tmp.write_bytes` or `os.replace` fails (for example disk full or permission error), the old blob stays on disk with the new metadata, so head() reports a content type and metadata that do not match the stored bytes. A crash between the two replaces leaves the same mismatch.
findings.suggestion: Write and replace the blob first, then the metadata. If the metadata write fails after the blob has been replaced, remove or roll back the blob, or accept that a stale-metadata window exists and document it.
findings.title: Metadata is replaced before the blob, so a failed blob write leaves inconsistent state
